subtopic: MAILING OF OLD AGE SECURITY CHEQUES

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MAILING OF OLD AGE SECURITY CHEQUES
speechtext:
1.	On what day of the month are old age security cheques put in the mail?
2.	Has consideration been given to mailing these cheques in time so that they will be received a few days in advance of the end of the month?
3.	If so, what is the result of such consideration?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: MAILING OF OLD AGE SECURITY CHEQUES
speechtext:
1.	On the last business day of the month.
2.	Yes.
3.	The decision to delay delivery of old age security cheques until the first few days of the month following the month the payment purports to cover was determined by the following considerations:
(a)	Old age security cheques are issued by the same offices and with the same equipment as are used for family allowances payments and sufficient time is not available after the closing-off of the family allowances cheque-run to permit the old age security cheques to be prepared and dispatched to the post offices in time for delivery to the payees several days before the close of the month. The alternatives would be (a) to advance the mailing date of family allowances cheques; or (b) to increase staffs and equipment so as to enable the preparation and delivery of the cheques by, say, the 28th of the month.
(b)	The banks are heavily engaged during the last few days of the month in handling
(Mr. Sinclair.]
government cheques in payment of salaries and wages of civil servants, war pensions, veterans' allowances, assigned pay of members of the armed forces, superannuation, and many other month-end payments, and it was accordingly felt that to add a further 650,000 cheques to this load would place an unreasonable burden on the banks.
(c)	The addition of a further 650,000 cheques to the month-end issue would overburden the cheque adjustment branch of the Department of Finance, which is already heavily taxed in clearing the existing month-end issues mentioned in (b).

subtopic: GRANT OF SUBSIDY
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS
speechtext: Would the minister explain just what -this amendment is?

subtopic: GRANT OF SUBSIDY
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
The provision in the act as it now stands is for payment by the federal government of 30 per cent of the cost, an initial payment to be made followed by four equal payments. It has been represented to us that some of the provinces might desire to make grants as well toward the establishment of cold storage plants and for that reason it was thought better to have a three-way split, one-third by the federal government, probably one-third by the province and one-third by those who were desiring to have the cold storage constructed. That was the reason for making it one-third instead of 30 per cent.
It must be remembered that this act was brought in in 1907 and was merely experimental at that time. It was thought best to have these payments spread over four years in order to keep some check on the charges that were made and on other regulations that might be applied to the operation of the plant. Our experience has indicated that there is no real advantage in that as these plants run for long terms of years. After four years there is no more control to be exercised by the fact that you are holding back money, although we still exercise the same control after the four years has passed.
It was thought by those who are benefited, particularly the co-operatives, that it would be of great help if the payment was made at one time thus doing away with the necessity to borrow money and pay interest thereon. So far as the government is concerned, it does not mean any more after we get into it a short time as the payments per year will be just about the same.

subtopic: GRANT OF SUBSIDY
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
I am not opposing the bill but as a matter of information will the minister state whether this was discussed
with the provinces before the legislation was brought in? Is it being done at their request or with their approval?

subtopic: GRANT OF SUBSIDY
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS
speechtext: There has been no relationship with the provinces in connection with this matter. It was discussed with cooperatives and others who are putting in cold storage facilities and it has been represented to us that some of the provinces might pay something toward these facilities. That is not any concern of ours; it is just a concern of the organization setting up the cold storage. However, they have suggested that if it was on a one-third basis a proper proposal for them to make to the province would be one-third from us, one-third from the province and one-third to be provided by the operator.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS

commodity in Saskatchewan. I was told last Tuesday, for example, that eggs were being sold at Sonningdale in the northern part of my constituency for as low as 8 cents a dozen.

speechtext: Consequently it seems to me that the provinces should be encouraged to build storage plants. If private interests such as the packing companies are going to receive assistance then it seems to me that the provinces should receive some federal assistance in the building of these plants.

subtopic: GRANT OF SUBSIDY
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR PAY- MENT OF UNPAID INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
I quite agree with the minister that it is a desirable change to have the subsidy paid in one instalment rather than as heretofore. As he has said, perhaps it has been embarrassing to the companies which have proceeded with construction, but his department has always had control in any event. There is one matter I should like to raise about which I am not certain, and I think it is one to which the department should give careful consideration. His department has had cases of applications for a cold storage subsidy where additions are being made to existing plants. The ruling by the department has been based upon an old ruling of the Department of Justice, and I might say to the Minister of Justice that, with respect, I think it is a ruling that is substantially in error. The ruling was that new construction or a new addition could not participate in any additional subsidy unless it was in a new building or an addition to the building. For instance, if you build a wing on a building and instal cold storage machinery therein then that cold storage machinery would qualify to receive an additional subsidy. In the particular case which was referred to the department a few months ago-and I notice the official who dealt with it is here and is listening-it was proposed to instal machinery for the purpose of cold storing vegetables in the basement of the United Fruit Company plant which had theretofore dealt specifically with fruit. No additional capital expenditure whatsoever was involved for the construction of a building and the department had to rule, basing itself on the old ruling of the Department of Justice, that since there was no additional structure or addition to the building the machinery did not qualify for an increased subsidy. It was admitted, however, that if an addition to the building had been installed the department would have been required to pay a much larger increased subsidy because the company could then qualify for the cost of the building as well as the machinery.
55704-205i

It seems to be a most unfortunate situation that a company which is trying to economize, both in its own expenditure and that of the department, in installing machinery in existing facilities, cannot qualify for a subsidy whereas if they had gone to the expense of building a new wing on their plant and putting the machinery in that wing they could have received a subsidy for both the machinery and the new wing. I would hope that the reference to a contract might obviate that. If it does not I suggest to the minister that he should give the matter very careful consideration, and possibly before the legislation is passed either he or his colleague, the Minister of Justice, might get a new ruling or amend the legislation so that it would be possible to make a new ruling. Otherwise it is a most unfair situation.

speechtext:
Well, I think we have got time as we started pretty early today. I quite appreciate the difficulty we are having now and I am all in accord with having something done about it. It certainly is a very deplorable situation at the moment. My good friend the Minister of Public Works is a man of infinite ideas but I would just make one or two observations about what I think might be improved around this place.
I appreciate that cabinet ministers with their drivers do not have the same problem as private members, which is all to the good, because I would hate to see a cabinet minister digging his car out of the snow here in the winter time. I do not think that would be proper.
We have these open parking lots and the snow piles up on the cars which are sometimes buried for days. Sometimes cars are frozen up here because of the fact that we lack electric plugs to keep them warm. maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal with a subject today which has been under consideration in the house on earlier occasions, and which is one that seems to call for increasing attention, in view of the extent to which other nations are looking to Canada as a source of raw materials for their defence requirements.

Conservation of Natural Resources
For many years we have been inclined to think of resources in this country as being inexhaustible; and for that very reason it took us a great many years to believe that there was any necessity in this country to introduce plans for the conservation of any of those great resources. Not long ago in the house a statement was made to the effect that we need not be greatly concerned about the raw materials that we were shipping out in large quantities.
I quote at this time the words used on June 3 by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), because it seems to me that they do draw our attention to a point of view which should be given careful consideration by the house. These are his words as they are reported at page 2855 of Hansard:
Fortunately we have an abundance of raw materials. I do not know of any material produced in this country that is in poorer supply today than when we first began export of the commodity. We all know that instead of a lower production of metals we have a higher production of metals. We all know that we have been able, by exploring and prospecting this rich country of ours, to become a very large scale exporter of iron ore which we formerly imported in almost our total requirements. We know, as we export that iron ore, that we are not depleting this country for future generations, because we have the commodity in abundance.
And shortly before that, in the same speech, the minister said:
Canada is immensely fortunate in that it is rich in those commodities the world needs and which the world is able to pay for, no matter what market conditions prevail in the have-not countries of the world.
Those words indicate that there is not yet in the minds of the government the belief that we need to conserve our resources in the face of the most unusual demands that we have been met with. In effect we are told that no matter what the demands by other countries may be, Canadians need not worry about expanding the export of raw materials because of their almost limitless quantity here in Canada.
It is true that our resources are enormous. Every hon. member of this house is aware of the extent to which exploration has expanded the knowledge of our available resources within these past few years. Nevertheless I suggest that it is wise for us at the same time to realize why it is that so many people from other countries have been pushing forward exploration and development of materials in this country. There is always the urge on the part of venture capital to seek new opportunities. That desire to find new places for investment undoubtedly would have produced extensive activities along that line in any event. However, there are other reasons why a great deal of this activity is being pressed forward. One of the main


reasons for activity in some particular lines of raw materials is that the use of raw materials in other countries in recent years has exhausted or come within a measurable distance of exhausting their own supply. For that reason new and increasing demands are being imposed upon Canada.
We can quite properly say that no nation with a population similar to ours possesses even comparable resources. Even without the qualification as to population it may be said that few countries with any population have as great resources as we possess. Probably the only countries in the world that have resources available for new development to the extent that we have here are Russia, the United States and Brazil. Even in the United States it may now be doubtful if they have resources available for new development on the scale that we have in Canada.
But there is a tremendous difference. Russia with her great resources has 200 million people and with a number of satellite nations dependent upon her for resources. The United States has approximately 160 million people. Brazil with great and still relatively undeveloped resources has more than 50 million people as compared with the 14 million living in Canada.
There is one very important reason why our position is different from that of any other country. We live next door to a nation of 160 million people who have attained the highest level of industrial production ever attained by any nation in the history of the world. They have attained a level of industrial production which has built up a very high level of prosperity that they will naturally seek to maintain in every way they can. It is in our interests as well as their own that they do maintain the standard of living they have been able to build up.
Our proximity to the United States places our resources in a very different position from those of Russia, Brazil and other countries with still undeveloped resources such as ours. For all practical purposes Russia is a self-contained unit except to the extent that under very rigid direction they may channel the movement of resources and trade within the total area of the Soviet empire.
Brazil is far from the great industrial centres of the northern hemisphere. Brazil is the natural base of supplies for a great many types of production for South America as a whole. Brazil has the markets of South America at her doors. Brazil has no other nation next door which is likely to feel the need for drawing supplies of raw materials

which the United States requires at this time and for which she will naturally turn to us as being the closest neighbour in a very substantial measure.
These facts create a unique situation so far as Canada is concerned. Our position cannot be compared with that of any other country in the world today possessing resources in any way comparable to ours. Immediately to the south and within a short rail haul lie the great industrial centres of the United States which have pitched their productive capacity to a level which they are not going to be able to maintain from the supplies of raw materials available within their own boundaries.
When this government points to the tremendous expansion in export trade which has brought to this country such apparent prosperity within the past few years it seems to ignore the fact that in a very substantial degree that export trade is based upon the exhaustion of raw materials in our two greatest markets for raw materials. We have seen an enormous expansion in our exports of raw materials to the United States. We have seen an expansion of our exports of raw materials to the United Kingdom. Export to the United States has increased to a much higher level proportionately than it has to the United Kingdom. We know that the demands being made upon us, and which we are very fortunate to be able to meet to the extent that we are, have largely been the result of the unhappy fact that the need for defence preparations has tremendously expanded the type of industrial production in both the United States and the United Kingdom which is based upon the utilization of the kind of raw materials that we possess in such tremendous quantities. That demand is going to continue. It is going to continue even if the demand for defence stockpiling should be greatly eased. It is going to continue because industrial production in the United States and the United Kingdom will call for metals and other raw materials on an increasing scale in the years ahead. It will call for exports on an increasing scale by virtue of the fact the United States is coming within measurable distance of exhaustion of its own raw materials in a number of lines.
If any country ever had an object lesson in the need for conservation and the careful use of its resources Canada has had that object lesson in seeing what has taken place in the United States as well as our own country in certain types of employment of raw materials. We Canadians are the last who should speak of raw materials as being inexhaustible. True, we have not exhausted any of our raw materials, so far as I know. We have, however,
Conservation of Natural Resources had the most unfortunate proof that raw materials can be exhausted, and it has been for that reason that during recent years so many Canadians have been urging effective plans for the conservation of the great forest resources of this country. The dominion government and the governments of most of the provinces have taken steps to encourage conservation of forest resources because of the convincing and unchallengeable evidence they have seen of the extent to which there can be a dangerous depletion of that particular type of raw material right here in our own country.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and most other hon. members in the house have seen in different parts of Canada ghost towns which once were prosperous communities. They are ghost towns for no other reason than the depletion or exhaustion of resources. Some of them are still ghost towns. Fortunately some of them have been revived by methods of conservation or by employment of other types of resources. One of the more dramatic examples of the exhaustion of resources and what it means to a community is to be found in the Dawson City of today. Once it was a thriving, prosperous and busy community in the Yukon which based its wealth upon the apparently inexhaustible gold available by placer mining in that area.
I can think of many other communities from the Atlantic to the Pacific which are ghost towns today or which have lost their prosperity because not merely forest resources but other resources were depleted to the point where they could no longer sustain the population which had once lived in prosperity in these communities. The fact that we may still have a large over-all supply of raw materials does not ease the situation for those who suffer directly from a situation of that kind. I am mentioning these instances because of the statement that seems to convey the thought that our resources are not exhaustible.
There are other features to the employment of our resources which should also be borne in mind. We have taken steps in this country to conserve our forest resources. The federal government has made some very positive advances in the conservation and protection of forest areas. The provincial governments in those provinces with great forest resources have devoted large sums of money and great effort to their conservation. That effort has produced positive and satisfactory results in many cases. I can think of a number of communities in the province of Ontario, as can the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which have been revived from almost total inactivity
3258	HOUSE OF
Conservation of Natural Resources by the introduction of new methods and the use of other types of wood. The fact that these efforts became necessary and have been crowned with success in no way diminishes the evidence of the danger of depletion of resources.
I would point out that the danger of exhaustion of forest resources is not as great as in the case of certain other resources because if there are wise plans of conservation our forests become a continuing crop rotating over long periods of years which can be maintained at an undiminished level if by the combined wisdom of the dominion and provincial governments cutting and reforestation plans as well as protective measures assure that continuity. This does not apply, however, to mineral resources which are gone forever once they are removed from the rock or soil in which they were originally found. For that reason even greater attention needs to be devoted to the conservation of our mineral resources. We have seen a number of cases where the exhaustion of minerals left empty buildings which today stand as tragic evidence of what occurs when any community that has been dependent upon raw materials of that type can no longer obtain those raw materials. What has happened in isolated cases can happen on a broad scale as well.
There is another aspect of this question which I would like to emphasize in discussing the use of our forest resources. One of the reasons that there has been such a demand for wood from our forests here in Canada is the depletion of the forest resources of the United States. The reason that we are called upon to export to the United States such enormous quantities of paper, of pulp, and of other wood products as well as cut wood itself is largely the fact that they have failed to conserve their own forest supplies. Perhaps it was impossible in a country with 160 million people to conserve their forest resources. We should remember, however, that if their forest resources in their large land area could not be maintained in such a manner as to meet their requirements, it certainly would be possible for us to deplete our resources if we continued to meet all their requirements in the years ahead without exercising the utmost caution and wisdom in the supervision of our forest resources.
However, there is a very particular reason which has a bearing on the utilization of our resources. Why do we now earn so much money from our wood products? Last year our forest products industry in this country earned nearly $1,100 million, a large part of that in the form of United States dollars coming into this country for the purchase of paper, pulp and other wood products-as


well as cut logs. The reason that we have built up this tremendous industry in Canada, and the reason that it is such a large earner of United States dollars as well as domestic dollars, lies in the positive policy that was adopted in this country in regard to the utilization of our forest resources.
Years ago it was decided as a matter of definite policy that we would follow a course which would encourage private enterprise to invest in the processing of cut wood in this country in a way that would create employment in Canada-employment at wage levels that are paid in industry using the raw materials. As a result of that we have seen the value of our forest products industry increase almost tenfold within a single generation. That is the direct result of a clear and definite policy of encouraging the manufacture, under private enterprise here in Canada, of wood products made from the trees cut in Canada. True, we have continued to export raw wood in many forms. It would appear that we are likely to continue that export for years to come. Canadians did, however, make a very simple decision. They decided that it was proper that Canadians themselves should benefit most from the use of the raw materials which Providence has placed at our disposal.
I cannot recall having heard or read of a single criticism, from what might be regarded as a well-informed quarter in the United States, of the adoption of that policy here in this country. True, there have been some criticisms of the incidence of that policy. I find, however, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has recently indicated in public statements that he approves of such steps as may be taken by those in Canada responsible for production which uses our forest products to obtain what they regard as prices which will adequately meet the demands for wages and other requirements here in Canada. While there has been a discussion of the price of newsprint and incidental details of that kind, I can only repeat that I am not aware of any case where anyone who might be regarded as well informed in matters of this kind has criticized Canada or has criticized Canadians for following the course of legitimate self-interest in this respect.
It seems to me that with the evidence we have that a policy of that kind can produce such striking and gratifying results in the case of the forest industry, we might well consider ways and means by which similar plans could be made for the utilization of our other resources to the highest level of employment here in our country.

When the United States found it necessary to turn to us for pulp logs to carry on their production of pulp, paper and similar products, they would have continued to supply their own mills with raw material from Canada and to have expanded the production in their own country instead of building mills in Canada if the same laissez-faire policy had been adopted in that case as has been adopted by this government in relation to our other raw materials.

speechtext:
There was no reason for the great pulp and paper producers in the United States to build mills in Canada if they could have obtained all the pulp logs they wanted simply by towing them across the great lakes at various points or carrying them by rail at other points in Canada. True, there would have been a pulp and paper industry here, but there is no hon. member in this house who is not aware that the reason for the tremendous increase in the production of paper in this country within the past few years, as well as the processing of pulp of various types and of other wood products, has been the encouragement of that industry through the various arrangements that were made with private industry under the legitimate direction of different governments within this country.
This subject now assumes a new relationship to the government of Canada at a time when, wisely or unwisely, the government has insisted upon renewing, in the years of peace, emergency powers which give it potential control over all of our resources. The Emergency Powers Act and the Defence Production Act, so long as they remain on the statute books, give this government a measure of control and a measure of direct interest, in our resources which might be employed in ways as yet unknown by any member of this house. I have indicated my own concern about the extent to which those powers have been carried forward into the years of general peace. Those powers have, however, been conferred upon this government, and this government has the authority to exercise them at any time. There are many other ways in which the dominion government now has a relationship with industry and the expansion of industry which it did not have in the past.
Through the various government agencies, it is called upon to co-operate with private industry, and under various plans it may be called upon from time to time to give financial assistance for the expansion of private industry, either for defence or for other purposes. For all these reasons, there are
Conservation of Natural Resources many ways in which the dominion government today would be able to make arrangements for the erection of mills and industries across this country which would utilize, at the highest and best paid level of employment, the raw materials which we have in such abundance. I can only repeat that we would not have had this tremendous pulp and paper industry in Canada, about which we hear so much today, had there not been some positive plans to encourage the great companies in the United States to build mills in Canada.
It is no answer to that statement to point out that the largest of the pulp and paper industries is a Canadian company, financed by Canadians. That company was able to carry out its financing and its expansion because of the general impetus given to this industry through policies of the kind I have mentioned. Within recent years large new plants have been erected right across Canada because of positive policies of this kind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when it was pointed out recently that there was a serious loss of our historic export markets in the United Kingdom for agricultural products of many kinds, we were answered with the statement that our exports to the United Kingdom, in dollar value, have been increasing during the past years and again within the past few months. It is true that we are exporting large quantities of materials required for defence production as well as other industrial production in the United Kingdom and the United States, It is true that the United Kingdom, as well as the United States, needs large quantities of nickel, aluminum, copper, zinc and other raw materials that we possess in such abundance. I need not go through the very long list of metals that we possess which today are in such great need, largely in other countries which at one time thought their resources were inexhaustible. They are being withdrawn at their present rate largely because of the failure to preserve the very rules of conservation which I am suggesting we should bear in mind here.
There is no reason why this country should be immune, over the years, from the same consequences as other countries have faced when they simply proceeded to use their resources without regard for the future. The answer that we are exporting a greater dollar value of exports to the United Kingdom is no answer to any farmer in this country. It does not in any way mislead him as to what has happened to our historic export markets in many lines. It obviously did not mislead the farmers of western Canada, and it has not misled farmers elsewhere. I hope no one will try to tell the dairy farmers that

Conservation of Natural Resources they can sell to the United Kingdom all that they can produce. I hope no one will try to tell the farmers who raise poultry, and who were exporting large quantities of their products, that they could sell all that they could produce to the United Kingdom. I hope that no hog raiser will be told he could sell as much bacon or pork to the United Kingdom as he could produce. I certainly hope that no cheese manufacturer will be told that we are still selling as much cheese as we were selling to the United Kingdom during the years past.
I say that I hope no attempt will be made to convince them, because I think that any attempt to do so would probably put in question the sanity of the person putting forward an argument of that kind. They know what has happened to their traditional markets. We all know that this year we will be selling hardly any agricultural products except grain and the cereals generally, as well as the meat that may be sold under the recent arrangement that was made between the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Canada. There is no mystery whatever about this increase in dollar value. Therefore, as we recognize the fact that countries which have exhausted their own raw materials are going to be looking for raw materials outside, this is the time for us to come to a clear understanding as to what our policy is going to be in the development and utilization of our own resources.
There are a number of other countries which have available supplies of raw materials similar to our own; but not many of them, if any, have the fantastic variety that we have here. Iron ore, copper, aluminum, uranium, zinc and many of the other metals and raw materials that we possess are to be found in many other parts of the world. There is a difference, however. There are many countries in the world with resources of raw materials of that kind which have not the fuel, the electrical energy, the highly developed communities nor the industrial skill to make use of those resources within the country concerned.
Most certainly we Canadians would not wish to see the United States in a position where its great industrial production would suffer for lack of raw materials. Most certainly we Canadians would not want to see any of those industries producing weapons or machines of defence held back in any measure because of shortage of raw materials for those industries and mills upon which we, as members of the western defence community, jointly depend. That consideration, however, does not change the over-all
	i
problem with which we are confronted. Where there is to be an increase in production of defence or other requirements, there is no reason to believe that in many cases that increase in production cannot take place just as well here in Canada as in the United States.
At the time when the United States was developing its industries from its own raw materials, during the latter part of the last century and during the early part of this century, I am not aware that at any time they hesitated to say that their first concern was the development of industry in the United States and the employment of citizens of the United States at the highest possible wages through the use of the raw materials which they themselves possessed. I am not aware of any occasion when the government of the United States felt that it was impelled to seek to place at the disposal of the industries of Europe raw materials which they could employ to their own advantage in the mills and the industries of the United States. The wealth, the strength and the population of the United States, and its pre-eminence as a world power today, have all come as the result of a clearly-understood policy that the first concern of the government of the United States at all times was not only to create employment in the United States for the citizens of that country already there, but also to create an expanding measure of employment which would make the largest possible use of the total resources-agricultural and forest as well as industrial.

that Providence had placed at the disposal of that single nation. Surely no citizen of the United States today could question the decision of any Canadian who decided that it is not only industrial employment with which we are concerned but employment of all kinds, and that we Canadians recognize that the best way to give greater stability to our agriculture in this country is to increase our population so that we have the largest possible domestic consuming market for the agricultural products which we can turn out.
Mr. Speaker, the figures of agricultural and industrial production suggest that we can well afford to recognize how vitally important the industrial development of this country is at all times to the agricultural population. There was a time, still within comparatively recent years, when we thought of this as primarily an agricultural country. Today we recognize that, while agriculture is our primary industry, the value of our industrial products now far exceeds that of our agricultural production. The figures showing the total value of agricultural production and of industrial production indicate the extent to

which we can create new demands for agricultural products of all kinds, by increasing the industrial and other employment across Canada through the widest possible utilization of our own resources.
When I say that, I am applying my remarks to all types of resources, but I particularly refer to those resources which have been so much before our eyes in recent years, and even perhaps more conspicuously in recent months. Canada has suddenly come to realize that it is one of the great producers of oil in the world, and that it has some of the greatest oil deposits known anywhere at this time. We have also come to realize that our oldest mineral industry in Canada, namely the iron industry, has new and almost unbelievable possibilities. Certainly those two resources- oil which today in its many forms is such an essential part of the development of our mcdern community and our whole industrial and commercial activity, and iron ore which is the foundation of the great industrial development of any country-have given us new and challenging opportunities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is happening in the case of iron ore will explain the point I wish to make generally with regard to resources, without limiting my argument in any way to that one raw material. I am not in any way seeking to minimize the importance of what has already taken place, nor am I seeking to minimize what the government has done in many respects to assist in that development. I am pointing out that under the unusual pressures which now exist and which will continue to increase, there is bound to be an ever-expanding demand for the resources we possess.
A new iron ore empire has emerged right across Canada. New towns are being built to house the workers both in the developments that are taking place and in the subsidiary activities growing up in those areas. There is a rapid increase in the production of iron ore, which means a great deal to this country.
Let us look at the figures. In 1946 our production of iron ore was 1,550,000 tons. By 1951 that had risen to 4,680,000 tons, and by 1955 it is said our production will be 20 million tons. That is a challenging story of expansion. But let us look at what this means in terms of steel made from the iron ore. In 1946 Canada produced 2,250,000 tons of steel, whereas last year we produced
3,445,000	tons. As has been explained in
Conservation of Natural Resources the house, an expansion is now under way which will increase production by another
1.150.000	tons. That would bring our total production up to approximately 4,600,000 tons.
Assuming that the expansion is even beyond what is now estimated and planned, that would mean that by 1955 we might be producing some five million tons of steel a year in Canada. And that is a great deal of steel. We are frequently told of the enormous expansion of steel production that is taking place. No one should seek to minimize the importance of that expansion. But the question we must ask ourselves, in view of these fantastic increases in the use and the supply of the raw material, is this: Is that enough? I submit the answer, definitely, is n-o.
In addition to the 3,445,000 tons of steel we produced in Canada last year, our imports jumped to 2,260,000 tons. That means that last year our use of steel for our own requirements amounted to approximately
5.700.000	tons. That does not take into consideration of course the steel machinery, the machine tools of all kinds, and other things which we imported but which we could have made here, if the steel had been available and we had gone into the production of these particular requirements.
We do see however that our requirements, on the basis of production plus imports of steel, alone, indicate that we used steel in 1951 substantially in excess of the amount that we will have available in 1955, under any plans which have yet been announced. This reduces itself to the simple proposition that unless there is a change in policy which does encourage greater expansion of steel production we are going to increase our production of iron ore by leaps and bounds at a time when we are also increasing the importation of steel made, in many cases, from that same iron ore which we export from Canada.
Merely by way of illustration, I recall the fact that today we are exporting iron ore from British Columbia to Japan, which returns in the form of steel ingots. We are exporting iron ore to the United States, and we see it returning in the form of steel to be used in industry in this country. We are exporting iron ore across the Atlantic also to be returned in the form of steel.
The important thing for all of us to remember is that at the same time we are exporting these raw materials, we are also exporting the most valuable asset this country possesses, and that is the young Canadians educated and trained here in our own country at the public expense, because those young Canadians are seeking employment elsewhere. In a great many cases they are

Conservation of Natural Resources leaving Canada to seek employment in those very industrial plants which are making finished products from the iron ore and other raw materials we export in an unprocessed state from this country.
These two problems go hand in hand; they must stand side by side to some considerable extent. Many Canadians were greatly disturbed, and there was a great deal of comment editorially and otherwise in the press, when an examination of the figures issued early this year by the dominion bureau of statistics indicated that while 591,000 people had come into Canada during the past ten years, 486,000 had left Canada in the same length of time. These were not 486,000 of the 591,000 who had come here. In most cases those 486,000 emigrants were young Canadians, born and educated and trained in this country, who were seeking employment elsewhere because of the higher wages offered in skilled activities outside Canada. That means that for every six people coming into Canada, five left. We paid a great deal of money to bring those people here. I am not questioning the wisdom of the policy which brings those people to Canada. I am pointing out, however, that those who left were young people with the training, character and skill that we want to keep in Canada by every possible method that we can adopt.
This it seems to me illustrates most forcibly what happens when we send our raw materials out and the highest level of employment in the use of those raw materials is elsewhere. Again may I say that I am not suggesting that we are not using our raw materials extensively; I am not suggesting that we are not increasing and improving our industrial production all along the line; I am simply placing these figures before us to indicate that there is a great deal more that we can do.
I hope that no one will suggest that I am placing before this house any argument that we should stop the export of our raw materials. I hope I have made it clear that I think we should export our raw materials in reasonable quantities, particularly those raw materials required to maintain the production of defence requirements. So long as we are not unreasonably depleting any of our own resources I see no reason why we should not maintain the export of such quantities of raw materials as will contribute to the maintenance of industrial production in other countries which are associated with us in our common efforts today. But I do think that if there is to be expansion in production related to the use of those raw materials, that expansion in production and employment should be here in Canada and not in some other country.


We have talked a great deal about keeping young Canadians in Canada and we have reason to talk about that. The best way to keep Canadians in this country is to do what we can to offer to them the most attractive type of employment that there is, to create for them in every way within our power under a free enterprise system the highest measure of employment in the most advanced stages of industrial production possible from the raw materials we possess. It is in work of this kind that so may of the new graduates in engineering, medicine and other technical branches of education feel that they can find greater opportunities in the United States today.
By all means let us send the last pound of raw materials that is needed for the production of those things required in this period of emergency in the common cause of the defence of freedom. If it can be used outside of Canada in this period of emergency, let it be sent to the places where it can best be used. But we should not encourage the export of a single pound of raw materials which is not necessary for that purpose or for the maintenance of the continued production of essential requirements in another country.
I have pointed out that most of these raw materials are available in many other countries which have not the same facilities for industrial production that we possess. This is something which is of interest not only to those who may possibly be employed in the steel or any other industry in Canada; it is a subject of primary concern to the farmer, to the office worker and to every other Canadian who benefits from the total volume of production and employment in this country. The more we fabricate in finished or highly processed form from our own resources, the more money we will earn as a people and the larger and more profitable will be the markets for our farmers, our fishermen and those who supply our basic food and other requirements.
I hope that nothing I have said will be interpreted as an argument in favour of any dog-in-the-manger policy. I am only suggesting that in the rapidly expanding development of resources opportunities for Canadians shall at all times be the first consideration of the parliament of Canada and of the people of Canada generally.
Nothing that I have said is a suggestion in any way that we should isolate ourselves from a world which more and more is bound up in trade. On the other hand, I do suggest that there are dangers which are before the eyes of every one of us and which are of particular significance to Canada, which depends so largely upon export trade. The

best kind of export trade we can have is the export trade that earns the most dollars for the volume of exports and at the same time creates the largest domestic employment so that the purchasing power of our industrial communities may advance the opportunities and prosperity of the whole of Canada.
We have lost our markets for many lines of agricultural production. We hope that they will return, but in the meantime the loss of those markets emphasizes the need for greater domestic markets. It emphasizes the need for increasing population in this country which can feed and support a population so far beyond that which we have today. The outstanding fact in this country at this time is that with virtually every raw material that is needed for expansion and production of all kinds, Canada lacks the most important natural resource of all, it lacks people. It lacks them in the number required to create internal markets which will cushion our economy against external disturbances. We particularly lack employment in sufficient quantity for those highly skilled occupations which attract the best brains from our universities and technical schools.
By the highest possible use of our materials for the development of industrial production in Canada we will make the most effective contribution we can to the maintenance of the human resources of this country which are so much more valuable than anything else we possess. I repeat that of all the resources, other than human, steel is the most important of the metal resources we possess. Of course it is not as important as food and the other basic requirements for our actual living, but for the purpose of creating employment it is the most important resource of all. With an adequate quantity of steel available, all other production can be expanded. With our resources of iron ore we have in Canada the brightest possibility of expansion we have ever had.
Because of the great abundance of all resources, we have taken those resources for granted. We have talked constantly about our limitless resources and have used that expression with some measure of justification. But in recent years as never before we have seen the depletion of resource capital throughout the world and we should now revise our ideas on this subject. There is no suggestion of criticism of this government alone. All Canadians, growing up surrounded by such an abundance of resources, have been inclined to dismiss from their minds the possibility that they could ever be used up. Nevertheless we know
Conservation of Natural Resources now that a number of countries are bankrupt in resources at this time. That kind of bankruptcy has not only reduced the status of nations in the past and in recent years but has destroyed civilizations in the past. Great opportunities are before us. With demands coming from all parts of the world for raw materials or the things made from raw materials, the decision for us to make with respect to what goes out of Canada is whether it shall go out in the form of raw materials or do we do everything possible to see that it goes out in the form of finished products?
Distant though the possibility of exhaustion may seem, there is every reason for us to remember that we are not immune from the dangers which have done so much to injure other countries when adequate measures of conservation were not introduced. It is with that thought in mind, and in the hope that, no matter who may have been responsible at any time in the past, we will now think particularly of the future, that I am presenting an amendment which I hope will be regarded as a positive proposal rather than as criticism of this or any other government. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada:
(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion:
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for employment and advancement of Canadians."

Mr. Speaker, with a great deal of what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said in the course of his speech I think all members of the house will find themselves in agreement. I think everyone here is conscious of the desirability of doing everything possible both by conserving our resources and by planning for their efficient use within Canada so that the citizens of Canada now and hereafter will enjoy the maximum benefits from the great heritage which is ours. Indeed, it is only within the last few years that many Canadians have begun to realize that this country is as richly endowed as it really is.

Conservation of Natural Resources
The recent discoveries of oil, uranium, minerals such as iron in Labrador, northern Quebec and Ontario, the new fields of nickel, copper, and so on, together with the development of the great natural resources in our waterpower, have at last led the people of our country to realize the extent of our resources and the possibilities that lie in them. I notice that the leader of the opposition has inserted in his amendment these words:
. . . this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will . . .
Then follow the various clauses. Let me point out that over the years it was under a system of free enterprise that such resources as it was recognized we had in this country were either neglected or exploited ruthlessly. If one wishes to see what unlimited, unrestricted free enterprise will do to a great resource all one has to do is to drive up the Ottawa and Gatineau valleys where once there were great stands of white pine from which the ships of the United Kingdom derived their masts and a great deal of the lumber that was required to build those wooden walls of Britain 150 years ago, to say nothing of the ships that we built ourselves on the great lakes and along the St. Lawrence river. Today one searches these valleys in vain for that mighty pine which once dominated them.
A few people made enormous fortunes. I need not mention their names because they are familiar to us in the streets and surroundings of the city of Ottawa, but nevertheless it was the free enterprise of these people that denied to this generation and to posterity a continuance of these mighty forests that once clothed the slopes of the Gatineau and Ottawa valleys.

I am making my own speech. If the hon. member does not agree with me he can rise later and tell me wherein I am wrong. All you have to do is to look across our country and the United States to see monuments to free enterprise in the wasteful exploitation of the great forest wealth of the North American continent. I have driven through Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, parts of Ontario and other places where once great forests grew and where free enterprisers have had unlimited opportunity to deny to this generation and those that succeed us the crop of trees to which they are entitled. I am very happy that today governments are stepping in and limiting free enterprise and are putting into effect conservation policies similar to those that they have had in the social democratic countries of Norway and Sweden, and even indeed in countries that are not social democratic such as Germany where an annual crop of lumber is now assured.
I know it is very difficult for governments to put such policies into effect. In my own province of Saskatchewan a royal commission was set up in 1944 or 1945 to go into the matter of conserving the forests of the northern part of that province. Their report was that with the rate of cutting then in effect there would be no saw logs left to cut within eight years. Therefore the government had to institute a conservation policy which was unpopular. Apparently it is understood now in the light of the results of the voting there in the last week, but at the outset it was unpopular, and any government which attempts to put conservation policies of that description into effect to ensure a permanent supply of lumber and to limit cutting to those trees that are ripe for cutting will have difficulties.
I welcome the resolution in so far as I am able to agree with it because it does to an extent focus the attention of this house upon the problem which confronts this country with its vast resources, particularly with its forest resources at the present time.
I say therefore that if you are going to do anything in the way of conservation you have got to say "Thou shalt not". That in itself is a limitation to private or free enterprise; and in respect of its reference to free enterprise I would, of course, have to oppose

this resolution. I do not agree that it can he done under private and free enterprise.
I am glad too that the governments of the various provinces, in co-operation with our own mines and resources department, have taken steps in recent years to prevent the loss of lumber and timber through fire hazards. I have noted that in all provinces there is a consciousness of the danger of fire and the loss which accrues to the provinces and to the country because of fire. We now have fire equipment in many parts of Canada to mitigate the evil effects of forest fires.
Then too there is the manner in which governments have tried to promote-and I will give some credit to the present government in this regard and to the provincial governments-conservation of the soil. After all, the most valuable resource we have in the long run is the top six inches of the earth's surface, which we call soil. I am one of those who fifteen years ago or thereabouts saw the effects of soil drifting-erosion by wind-due to some extent to the dryness of the soil and to some extent to faulty methods of cultivation. It was also due to overcultivation of the soil. We saw the soil blowing across the lands in such quantities that in the middle of the day in some of our western cities one had to turn on the headlights of a car in order to see where one was going. However, because of the experience and because of the encouragement of governments, that has to some extent been stopped. New methods of cultivation have been adopted-summerfallowing every year, leaving the soil in a lumpy condition instead of working it down like a nice garden so that it will blow-has all helped in recent days to prevent erosion of that description. Governments have encouraged contour plowing of the land-around the hills instead of up and down-so that when the rains come the soil is not washed down into the rivers, lakes and seas.
With soil conservation we have in this country a resource that will last for ages. European countries have demonstrated that soil can be cultivated not for hundreds of years but literally for thousands of years where proper methods are put into effect. On the other hand, parts of Africa, and parts of Asia have demonstrated to us that without careful methods of cultivation and without irrigation, lands which once grew great crops of fruits, grain and foodstuffs can be turned into the deserts of Mesopotamia or the deserts of North Africa. Anything that the government can do to conserve the top six inches of soil and to encourage its proper cultivation, and with that the conservation of water
Conservation of Natural Resources so that when necessary the water can be used to replenish moisture in the land, is well worth putting into effect and supporting.
I quite agree with the leader of the opposition that these forest resources, the soil and so on, will eventually be worth far more to this country than the wasting resources. Once you have found gold and have taken it out of the ground you have nothing left but a hole in the ground. I remember that not very far from where I was born, 2,000 years ago vast quantities of tin were mined and shipped by the Phoenicians-

I meant that I had read about it. Probably I phrased my remarks a little awkwardly and I did not intend to imply that I have either that age or the wisdom that goes with it. But there the old mines, the holes in the ground, remain. They are worked out and very little tin now is found where once great quantities were mined.
With respect to wasting resources such as oil and minerals which we have, as the leader of the opposition said, recently we have learned of further great resources of that basic mineral-iron ore in Labrador and iron ore in northern Quebec. I would like to see as much of that iron ore as possible processed in this country and utilized for the building of industry in this country. I do not know just what encouragement the leader of the opposition would give but I would point this out. Over the years the government of Canada has given a tremendous amount of encouragement to industrialists to utilize our resources within this country. We were for many years one of the highest tariff countries in the world, protecting Canadian industry, and I am sometimes inclined to blame Canadian capitalists who, at that time under the guarantee of domestic free enterprise and behind high tariff walls, had the opportunity of doing a great deal to develop industry in this country but did not do so. I do not think that today, if I may interject this thought, we can afford to grant that kind of protection for the building up of industries that will utilize our natural resources. In the kind of world in which we live we have to sell things to get dollars, as the leader of the opposition put it, into the country. The only way in which we can try to do that is to export goods and receive in return goods which nations can send to us for consumption or, perchance, export to third parties from whom they or we can receive goods in order to maintain our export industry and our trading position. Consequently, I cannot agree that any encouragement should be forthcoming or can be forthcoming to Canadian

Conservation of Natural Resources industry if that involves any raising of the tariffs in any new measure of protection. That is a point upon which I would like my hon. friends to my right to comment when they rise to participate in this debate.
The reason great iron resources of Canada are now being searched for, and where found are being developed by American capital is that they have wastefully mined a good deal of their iron resources in their country. We know, of course, of the Mesabi range in Minnesota and Wisconsin. It has been said that had that range been mined more carefully the resource would have lasted much longer.
However, be that as it may, we have other resources that were not particularly mentioned which I should like to mention before I speak of the human resources, one of which is fish. We should conserve our fisheries, and I hope that more will be done to conserve the coastal waters fisheries and also the fisheries in our inland lakes and rivers. We have a fine source of wealth in the fresh water fish that can be found all across Canada, in the Northwest Territories and south of them, in almost every province. They form a rich source of food supply, as well as a wealth of employment and industry.
Then, of course, for a time we were in danger of having our fur-bearing animals severely depleted. When the leader of the opposition was speaking I looked up the conservation policies that have been put into effect in my own province since 1944. In that year the beaver in the province were almost extinct, and only 473 beaver were trapped. A conservation policy was put into effect, as with muskrats and other fur-bearing animals, and only a certain number of animals were allowed to be taken in certain spots. As a result, in 1951 the trappers were allowed to take 14,078 beaver, and still leave behind plenty of breeding stock. All this was accomplished in the short space of about seven years. Of course, it involved transferring a few beaver, which were making nuisances of themselves in the southern part of the province into regions where they could live and breed freely without doing any injury to the surrounding countryside. All these are resources that are worth conserving. The provinces, together with the Department of Resources and Development, have an obligation to conserve these resources, to put in the proper conservation policy, and incidentally I hope that the members of all parties in this house will support such a move.
A government which sets out to put conservation policies into effect, to say to trappers that they cannot trap except in certain areas and in certain quantity, is going to have


difficulty. The same thing is true when you say to fishermen that they cannot fish in certain lakes until they have been cleaned of disease. You are going to have difficulty, because it takes a few years for the people who are affected to realize that this is being done in their own interests. I realize that in those few years there may be elections and seats may be lost in the areas in which these conservation policies are put into effect. Consequently, I should like to see such conservation policies supported by all parties in this house, and not made matters of political controversy or of political division.
The concluding portion of the speech by the leader of the opposition was one which struck a very responsive note in my mind, and that was his reference to the conservation of human resources. It is not only the loss of our young people abroad that is vital in that regard, but the death rale among the population of Canada, or some parts of it, is equally vital.
Last week I was staggered when I was told that until hospitals and schools had been put into the north regions of Saskatchewan since 1944 the infant mortality in that particular area-not the whole of it but in quite a large area-was no less than 50 per cent. One half of the children died before reaching one year of age. Today, of course, hospitals, schools, education and so on have tended to reduce that death rate until, while it is above the normal average for the country, it has been greatly reduced. The health of our people, therefore, is a question that should be faced very freely. I was reading an article in the current issue of Maclean's magazine a few days ago concerning the high cost of medical care, the high cost of hospitalization and so on in this country. Until we bring hospitalization and health facilities so close to the people that they can be used as freely as our children use the public and separate schools in our country, we shall not have put into effect a human conservation policy such as we should have in Canada.
The leader of the opposition mentioned the tragic loss of many of our ablest young university students, who cross to the United States because they think there is a better opportunity there. In January, I had the opportunity of addressing the social science group of the University of Chicago. On Sunday morning when I went down to the university chapel, I was invited to lunch by the Canadian students. I found twenty-seven of them in that university, and all were interested in Canada. While I was unprepared to do so, they asked me to tell them something about the opportunities that were likely to be presented to young people in this country

in the days to come. I told them that while I thought, at the moment, if they came back to Canada they might have to take a slightly lower salary or wage than they might receive at the moment in the United States, I was convinced that five or ten years from now, when they had trained themselves to fit into the economy of our country, they would be in a better position in Canada than they would be in five or ten years in the United States. I believe that is so. I strongly advised them to come back.
I outlined, off the cuff as it were, what was happening in this country today. I told them of the great aluminum and power developments as well as the pulp and paper development in the province of British Columbia; the development of the great oil resources of Alberta; the hunt for oil in Saskatchewan and the finding of uranium and other minerals in that north country; Manitoba, with its nickel and other resources; Ontario, with its mineral wealth, its power resources and other resources; Quebec, with the tremendous resources in northern Quebec and Labrador and so on.

Consequently private enterprise, working in the interests of the private investors alone without regard, as is often the case, to the safeguarding of the rights of the masses of the people, will not develop our resources in the manner in which they should be developed. I say quite readily to the leader of the opposition and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that there is a place for private enterprise in the development of our resources; but I do not think you can leave the development of our resources wholly to private enterprise, as this resolution implies. It says, "a national policy under a system of free enterprise". That is the quarrel I have with the resolution.
If I may do so, Mr. Speaker, in order to put our viewpoint clearly before the house, I want to move an amendment to the amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles);
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom the words "under a system of free enterprise and"
It would then read:
this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada;
(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for employment and advancement of Canadians.
I move that as an amendment to the amendment, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That makes it a good resolution.

maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes; that makes it a better resolution.

maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this discussion has been, I think, timely and one which should attract considerable interest throughout the whole house and throughout the country. I am keenly interested in it because, during my short life, I have witnessed the almost wanton destruction of certain of Canada's great resources; and I think it is time that something really worth while be done by way of conservation and intelligent development.
The speeches which have been made this afternoon on the amendment have been, I think, most revealing and a good many suggestions have been put forward. On reading the amendment I find myself in much the same position as that of the hon. member for

Conservation of Natural Resources Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I was just a bit puzzled about the use of that term "under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces". I have always championed the cause of private enterprise, and I shall continue to do so because I believe it is the best way in which to induce the utmost from human beings. I think that under no other system can the proper inducements be offered. For that reason I would go along with the resolution and with what has been said about it, with the following reservations. Mr. Speaker, I believe that in the development of our great resources there must be laid down fundamental policies that will definitely result in proper conservation as well as development. I do not know whether you would call that a plan. If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would like to call it a plan, that is fine; but I think that is policy. I think the difference between "plan" and "policy" may be infinitesimal, but I prefer to look upon it as a policy laid down by the representatives of the people and adhered to carefully by the administrative part of government.
I think that experience of the past will show that under a system of the kind of free enterprise to which we have consigned our resources, waste, destruction and depletion have resulted; I do not think there is any question about that. If we are to conserve those resources as they ought to be conserved, I believe that we must keep title in government; I mean to say that the ownership of the resources themselves should reside in the provincial governments. I do not see any other way of administering a careful scheme or policy of development along with the necessary conservation.
That is the experience that we have had in our province. We find that if the province retains the title to the resources and does not give individuals or corporations large acreages, large slices or large concessions-that is, give them outright-we then have some sort of control by which we might regulate carefully future development and conservation. It therefore seems to me that the first and most important part of any national policy of development of resources should be the determination to keep ownership residing in government which, of course, in this case would be the government of the province.
In the second place we believe that it is wiser to have the developmental work done by private enterprise regulated under a government system of leases, rentals and royalties whereby, through a specific contract, there might be careful supervision. If the contract is not lived up to in all details,

we feel that the contract should be taken away and perhaps given to other individuals or private enterprises which are prepared to do the job as it ought to be done.
That is the experience which we have had in the province in which I reside; and it has proved itself many times over. Not only has it proved wise from the point of view of conservation and orderly development but, in addition, it has proved wise in that we have been able, from our resources, to recover a substantial share of the proceeds for the people themselves who own those resources. Somehow or other governments in the past have had the idea that in order to get development you had to give great big slices of our various resources to certain individuals or corporations to induce them to develop them. That is not so. That was the policy, I think, for a good many years; and I am just afraid that a great many political heelers have benefited as a consequence of the feeling that the party owed them something, that they have thus been able to get large slices of our resources and have gone ahead to develop them as they wanted to develop them, without any thought for future generations.
If government keeps title and if government therefore lays down a definite and specific policy for the orderly development and the conservation of those resources, we feel that adequate supervision can be given and that there will be something left for the generations yet unborn.
That is the way we have proceeded with our oil development, that is the way we are proceeding with our timber development, and so it will be with the tar sands and other resources that are now just coming into some prominence. If that is the kind of thing which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has in his mind when he moves this resolution, I find that I can go along with him quite well. But if he means that we shall continue, as in the past, to grant by gift or title certain substantial slices of our resources to anybody for development, then I cannot go along with him at all because that is not the way to get conservation.

Yes, I certainly can.
