speechtext:
Conservation of Natural Resources country in connection with the preservation of wild ducks and wild geese. At the same time they are helping to conserve water supplies, and to store it for the use of people in those areas. In addition we have other demonstrations such as those being carried out by the Jack Miner foundation at Kingsville. Sometimes I wonder if such projects are receiving the encouragement they merit. I am doubtful about it. While I am not in possession of the whole story, from what I have observed I can say that these demonstrations are very much worth while and are doing a great deal to preserve for future generations the benefits to be derived from maintaining the numbers of those wonderful old game birds that, through the years, have been wantonly destroyed.
I wonder if we are taking sufficient care to see that such demonstrations as are put on are given proper encouragement. Correspondence I have received would seem to indicate that the Jack Miner foundation and perhaps some others in Canada are not just as affluent as they might be. It looks to me as though some of them are in real danger of encountering financial failure, through lack of public support. These are matters concerning all people, not just a few of them. It seems to me we ought to be paying much more attention to the success of these wildlife conservation schemes that have been going on for so many years on a basis of voluntary private enterprise. I would not want to see any of them fail.
A word now about our human resources. I agree we are losing too many of our educated young men and women, and I believe some of that loss can be traced to higher salaries in other countries, notably in the country to the south. It may be traced to better working conditions that exist in other countries, but that is not all. I am sure careful investigation will show that there are some very stupid professional policies being followed right here in Canada, and I want to cite one of them.
I have in mind a bright young fellow who finished high school in 1946, the year after the war ended. It will be recalled that young returned men were making application for entry into the universities of Canada and, as was proper, they were given priority. This young man applied to every university in Canada at which the professional course which he wanted to take was taught. He was told that their classes were full, that they were giving priority to returned men and therefore he could not get in.
He did not want to waste a year or two, so he applied to several universities in the United States and was finally accepted, I


think by one in southern Idaho. He went down there, took his course and after graduation came back to his native land to practise pharmacy. There was a scarcity of pharmacists in Ontario, and I understand also in other provinces. He applied for a licence to practise and although the pharmaceutical association were quite prepared to admit that his qualifications were as good as those they required for a licence in Ontario, they would not let him have a licence until he had first obtained one from his own home association, which in his case was in the state where he had finished his university training. That was the situation in every province in Canada where this young man applied for a licence.
He then had to go back to the United States; but before he could obtain a licence to practise there he had to renounce his Canadian citizenship and apply for United States citizenship. Having done that and having passed his examination in the state and received a licence, he found that before he could obtain a licence in Canada he would have to wait five years before he could regain his Canadian citizenship, working for low wages as a pharmaceutical assistant during that time.
This is characteristic of the stupid policies we have in Canada by which many professional bodies are bound. These professional bodies are doing a whole lot to add to the losses we are sustaining in bright young men and women who are graduating from our universities. These young men want to live in this country, they want to work here and help to develop our country. It seems to me that we ought to be coming to our senses and doing something to conserve our human resources.
I agree with the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that our young people are of paramount importance and that everything possible should be done to introduce health schemes in the provinces throughout Canada which will give our young people a chance to live abundant lives free from disease and disability.
Finally I want to say that during the discussion of this important topic this afternoon I have not heard anyone refer to the fact that the great waster of our resources at all times has been war. Sometimes we overlook the fact that wartime is when we deplete our resources, especially our mineral and forest resources. Notorious as war has been as a wanton waster, we are doing very little to correct the situation. It seems to me that the best conservation scheme we could possibly work out would be one which would get at and remove the causes of war. When

we do that I am satisfied that we will not then have to run the dangers that we have been running of depleting the valuable resources which are Canada's. We should be able to root out and cure these basic causes, and there are basic causes.
When that happens we can turn our attention to other schemes of conservation such as the one I have outlined, under which the provincial governments on behalf of the people would retain title to the resources, which, in turn, would be developed under a policy of private enterprise, regulated and supervised by the government. If the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) indicates that that is the thing he had in mind when he said "under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces" then I would say we will support his amendment.

Mr. Speaker, there are quite a number of people at the lakehead who are interested in the development of our natural resources which in that vicinity are of two types, pulp and paper and mining. I must say that I was considerably heated up when a communist member of the provincial government at Toronto came up to Port Arthur and told us we should have a smelter at the lakehead. Using his own words, there was no reason why we should not have a smelter there.
I have inquired about this from several people who are interested in the Steep Rock mine and they tell me the reason we do not have a smelter at Steep Rock or at the lakehead is that the iron ore is of high quality and in order to make it of commercial value it must be mixed with a lower grade ore. That is one reason. The other reason we do not have a smelter at the lake-head is that we are too far away from markets or from sources of power in the form of coal or gas. We are told that gas is on the way to Fort William from Alberta, and if that comes through we are more likely to have a smelter at the lakehead. When that happens I am sure the right hon. minister and myself will be very pleased.
Our other main natural resource is pulp and paper. We hear a great deal about the amount of pulp being shipped to the United States, but I think these statements are exaggerated. I made some inquiries a few minutes ago and found out that very little pulp is shipped out of British Columbia. Perhaps more is shipped out of Alberta, but I am informed by a prominent pulp and paper man at the lakehead that not more than 5 per cent of the pulp produced there is shipped to the United States. Let me indicate how true that statement is.
Conservation of Natural Resources
We have two mills at Fort William, one of them having the largest paper machine in the world. The two big machines in the Great Lakes Paper Company have the greatest production record of any mill in Canada. There are two pulp and paper mills at Port Arthur; there is one at Dryden, one at Nipigon, one at Terrace Bay, one at Marathon and one at Heron Bay. These mills employ thousands of men in the bush and in the mills themselves.
I say that our record in the development of resources at the head of the lakes is splendid, so much so that I think we can tell the rest of Canada and the rest of the world how it can be done. I know we cannot develop and manufacture all our natural resources. We cannot process our gold for the market. We must export some of our wheat, and we are sorry we have to ship some of our barley to the United States for a purpose that is perhaps not in the best interests of the citizens of that country. At the lakehead we think our natural resources are being used to do a big job in developing our country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I missed the first part of the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I came into the house when he was discussing conservation of our natural products. To begin with, perhaps I might say a word on that subject.
The natural products that we export can be divided into groups. Our field crops include wheat, oats, barley, and also timber, for timber is also a crop. I think we are all interested in making sure that our ability to grow these crops is protected to the full. Our grain crops for export are grown chiefly in the prairie provinces, and the federal government and the three prairie provinces have for many years devoted close attention to protecting the ability of the soil of these three provinces to produce cereal crops. These crops are used in Canada to the extent that they are required for human consumption and feed in this country and of course the balance is exported. I am sure there can be no objection to that type of export of our annual crops.
I might point out that the natural resources of this country are owned by the provinces. The federal government can assist the provinces to protect the ability of the soil to produce, but it cannot direct the methods of production. The federal government is responsible for the export marketing of the products, but the regulation of production methods is primarily for the provinces. Again it is the provinces which own the metals, the petroleum and the other mineral resources

Conservation of Natural Resources of Canada. So far as forests are concerned, there again the policy of forest management is for the provinces to determine. Each province has a policy. In my opinion some are better than others, but I think that by and large all the provinces are attempting to do a good job of forest management. Part of the task of forest management is to make sure that cutting does not overtake natural growth. Forests are a crop that matures every twenty to forty years, and each province is responsible for seeing that the cutting does not exceed this respective rate of reproduction. I do not know whether it was true, but I am told that up to a few years ago the toll of the forests taken by fire and by destruction through overage was about equal to the cutting. I hope that situation is not true today. However, we know that in addition to the harvesting of the forests there is a very considerable loss by fire and by allowing trees to become overage. There again I believe a fair job is being done in protecting the forests. In that respect the federal government is also making considerable expenditures, and I believe it is doing a reasonable job in helping the provinces to do what is primarily their job.
Then we come to minerals. There again mineral leases are granted by the provinces, and the federal government takes an active part in promoting the production of minerals and in improving methods for the treatment of those minerals. The suggestion was made that we are exporting too great a proportion of our production of mineral wealth. I doubt If that is true. We use in Canada the larger part of mineral production from Canadian soil. For instance, at the present time we are fabricating in Canada about 60 per cent of our production of copper, approximately 50 per cent of our production of zinc and a considerable proportion of our production of lead. The balance is going to countries that are joined with us in defence preparations, and our present markets in those countries are really an expansion of our normal markets, the larger demand arising from the needs of war production.
I was interested in a statement by the leader of the opposition which I hope I wrote down correctly. He said that not a pound of our metals not required for defence or for the normal needs of another country should be exported. I think we can be a little more generous than that. Canada has been and still is dependent on other countries for metals that are vital to this country, and other countries do not limit us to the amount that we need for defence or for the normal purposes of this country. They deliver to us what this country needs. I suppose as good an example as one can find is aluminum. We are one of the world's great exporters


of aluminum. What part of aluminum originally comes from Canadian soil? None of it. The only thing that we contribute to the manufacture of aluminum is electric power. The principal ingredient of aluminum is bauxite. Canada imports bauxite from British Guiana, from Jamaica and from French Africa. Another ingredient of aluminum is cryolite, which we import from Greenland. Another is limestone. We used to obtain it from Newfoundland before Newfoundland became part of the dominion, and we still obtain it from Newfoundland. Therefore I should say that we contribute both power and limestone to the manufacture of aluminum. Well, you can say that these countries are robbing their own resources by shipping all this bauxite to Canada. It is true that some day British Guiana is going to be depleted so far as bauxite is concerned; nevertheless when we discuss our own policy with respect to the exporting of raw materials it is well to realize the dependence of Canada on the raw materials of other countries.
I have a few figures with regard to our principal imports. Let us take crude rubber. In 1951 we imported crude rubber to the value of $65 million. We imported raw cotton to the value of $94 million and raw wool to the value of $95 million. We imported coal and coke from the United States and thus depleted their resources to the extent of $190 million last year. We imported petroleum last year to the extent of $354 million. We talk about how careful we must be not to overproduce but we are only producing about one-third of the petroleum requirements of this country. In the next ten years we hope we can raise the one-third to one-half, but the consumption of petroleum in Canada is rising almost as fast as production in this country is being increased.
We have imported other raw materials too: molybdenum, manganese, and tin. We have no source of supply of those products native to Canada. We are dependent on other countries to see that our requirements for them are met.
It is said that the United States has been built on the basis of self-interest; that the United States never exported to Canada or anywhere else any material that they needed at home. Now, let us examine that for a moment. In the last war supplies of petroleum were very short indeed. Every motorist in the United States and every motorist in Canada was rationed, and rationed severely; but the United States never withheld supplies from Canada that put the

Canadian user of petroleum in any worse position, than United States users of petroleum.

That is again the opposite to the suggestion of the United States looking after themselves first.
In the case of sugar, it was in short supply during the last war. The United Kingdom controlled all the empire sources of sugar, but the United Kingdom made sure that Canada got the sugar needed and that Canada fared just as well as her own people or the people in any other part of the empire. That was true of manganese. Our sole source of manganese at that time was South Africa, and there again the United Kingdom made sure that Canada had the manganese we needed. Tin we get partly from empire sources and partly from other sources. There again those responsible for the distribution of tin were not Canadians; nevertheless they made sure that Canada got her full share of tin when tin was in short supply.
Now we in turn have been trying to do our share in looking after the metal requirements of the free world. We had a very heavy responsibility in the matter of nickel. Before the second world war we supplied 90 per cent of all the nickel used in the world, and today I suppose we supply about 85 per cent. True, we have been depleting our resources of nickel. In the last war we had only one source of supply. Today we have many. Why? Because in an effort to keep up with the enlarged requirements- and we are mining more nickel than at any previous time in our history-we have opened up other sources of nickel. We are building a railroad into Lynn Lake where there is a very important deposit. I am told there are other discoveries in that vicinity which promise to make northern Manitoba as large a source of nickel as Sudbury. Plans are under way to open up a nickel deposit in British Columbia. We all know that Falcon-bridge, also operating in the Sudbury area, is bringing in three new properties at the present time. Are we really depleting our

Conservation of Natural Resources nickel resources? True, we are mining great quantities of nickel; but the fact that we are using great quantities of nickel has stimulated exploration and from exploration has come development with the result that Canada is far richer in known deposits of nickel today than it was when the great demand of the second world war came upon that industry.
The same is true of other metals. Copper, in this country, has been a by-product metal. It has always been mined as a by-product of nickel or as a by-product of gold. There again the present great demand for copper has turned our prospectors to exploration for new deposits of copper. The result is that we have located a tremendous body of lower grade copper ore in the Gaspe peninsula. An enormous development of copper, for copper alone, is to be undertaken in that area. We also know of other deposits of copper which can be brought in as demand requires.
The production of zinc has been stepped up by about 35 per cent since the preparedness program began, and we know now it can be stepped up to almost any known requirement. Again, exploration has stepped ahead as demand has been stepped up.
I might mention the rarer metals as well. For example, in the last war there was a strong requirement for tungsten. There was a known deposit of tungsten in the country and, as private enterprise was not prepared to develop it, the government stepped in and opened the Emerald tungsten project. A mill was set up there and, in the course of several months, we provided sufficient tungsten to turn a shortage situation into a situation of oversupply. When the war ended the government thought it had a high cost tungsten deposit on hand and as there was also lead and zinc on the property which might be developed it seemed good business to sell the property to private enterprise. When the Korean situation came along the government bought back that property at exactly what it had sold it for. Further exploration has indicated that the tungsten deposit being worked during the last war was underlain by a much richer deposit, and today the government has a mine of rich tungsten ore that will stand up and be competitive in peacetime as well as in wartime. We are able to supply friendly nations with tungsten, and that at this time is a very great contribution indeed. I suggest in mining that tungsten we are not depleting the resources or Canada. When the present supply is used up we know that we have several other deposits of tungsten, and we are sure we can

Conservation of Natural Resources meet any requirements the world may have for tungsten for decades to come.
The same is true of cobalt. It was assumed that all the cobalt had been mined in this country years ago. The town of Cobalt was built on the mining of cobalt and the mines were supposed to be worked out. When cobalt became a scarce metal in this war we went back into that area and have been producing cobalt there on a very extensive scale, a scale that has in fact enabled us to remedy the world shortage of cobalt. Today cobalt is no longer a metal that is embarrassing war production.
I could go on and mention other metals. I might take uranium, which is a metal in tremendous demand. We were mining it before the last war but the mine had been closed down and was flooded. When the demand grew for uranium the government bought that property and proceeded to open it up. I may say the known resources of uranium in that particular mine are considerably greater today than the known resources were at the time the property was acquired. Prospecting for uranium has brought to light other deposits, not as rich but tremendously more extensive. The government and a number of private industries are engaged in bringing in uranium metal as a very large scale development.
The amendment states, in part, that in association and collaboration with the provinces the dominion should promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada. I suggest we are doing that very thing at a rate that has never been equalled. We are not only taking care of the requirements of the people of Canada, but we are able to make a substantial contribution to the requirements of other countries.
For a moment let us examine the position of the United Kingdom under the policy laid down by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). He believes that we should supply the defence requirements of a country together with sufficient metal for its normal requirements, but not a pound more. The United Kingdom is in the most difficult position of any country in the world today. It is without raw materials. It is true that there are raw materials within the empire, but not within the United Kingdom. The only raw material that the United Kingdom has in any considerable quantity is coal. The people of the United Kingdom are only able to produce about 60 per cent of the food they consume. Their task is to make their living by importing raw material from other parts of the world, fabricating that material into finished

goods and exporting the finished goods in exchange for other raw material and for food.
The leader of the opposition made the statement that England has metals in other parts of the world. It is true that Britain has metals in other parts of the world. Why does she not obtain metals from those sources?
I am sure that in the position in which Britain is today, if she could obtain them from a sterling area she would do so in preference to paying dollars for these metals. If more copper could be obtained from Rhodesia-and there is plenty of copper there-that is where it would be obtained. Some is obtained there. If more zinc, lead and other metals could be obtained from other possessions-and there is plenty of zinc and lead in other parts of the British empire-they would be obtained from those sources. Britain is obtaining all that can be obtained from those sources, and is buying from Canada just as she has always bought from Canada because her requirements cannot be filled by other parts of the British empire alone. We are supplying metal to Britain. She has always been the principal customer for our copper and zinc, and still is our principal customer. So long as Britain requires copper and zinc from Canada, I believe it will be the policy of the present government to see that she gets that copper and zinc.
I may say that we have given preference to the requirements of the United Kingdom in that regard, and we have refused to permit our exporters to send copper to the United States or elsewhere to an extent that will deprive Britain of her full requirements from this country. We took that action because Britain is our historic market, and we have endeavoured, during periods of shortage, to protect our historic customers.
The amendment further states that we should protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion. I believe the provinces are doing a fair job of protecting the productivity of the soil so far as grains and timber are concerned. I suggest that so far as minerals are concerned, we have a very long way to go and very many decades to pass before there will be any shortage of any metal that Canada is producing today.
The amendment states also that we should expand our industrial production. We have been doing that. In each year since the war Canada has never invested less than 20 per cent of our national income in new development. Last year we spent about 24 per cent of our national income in capital investment. I know of no other country in the world that has managed to spend as much as 20 per cent of its national income for that purpose. Last year we spent in permanent investment, that

is in machinery, in factories, for everything of a permanent nature that we build in Canada, about $4,400 million. This year the expenditure in capital improvements will probably exceed $5 billion. There is a limit to the proportion of its national income that any country can afford to put into capital investment. I wish we could afford to go at a faster pace. I wish we were geared to move at a faster pace, but we have been gearing ourselves to move at an ever faster pace each year.
The first year after the war our total investment in capital improvements was about $3 billion, and this year we expect to be able to spend about $5 billion in capital investment. Provided this country continues to prosper, we will spend larger sums each year in the development of the resources of this country.

I believe many people were both startled and shocked to learn at that time, as a result of information emanating from the council meeting, that there had not been on any broad scale in any of the countries of the NATO community any real survey or inventory of the economic resources then available to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It is true there might have been some semblance of an inventory; but some of the most caustic observations at that time were directed to the fact that no proper inventory had been made setting out the resources of the free countries of the world. When it is said that there was no proper inventory, it will be suggested that such a statement could be made only in a matter of degree, and that there had been some inventory. The fact remains that this critical comment was made on that occasion, and it was those comments which prompted the proposal I made in my speech in the house on October 22, 1951.
While I am not seeking to commit anyone at this time to the proposals I then made, I might point out that they were presented in an effort to be constructive. I was convinced then, and I am still convinced, that there is work for a board or a commission, whichever one may choose to call it, which would deal with our natural resources. The name to be applied to such a body is not important; the important thing is what the body does, the purposes for which it is set up and the extent to which it achieves its objectives.
On the occasion to which I have referred I made these suggestions:
That appropriate legislation be introduced setting up a national development production board to be composed of representatives of government on the federal and provincial levels and of agriculture, industry and labour and other branches of our national endeavour, to achieve the following objectives :
(a)	To survey at once the natural resources of Canada in relation to their availability and the foreseeable demands as presently indicated by the requirements for our defence program, the anticipated demands arising from our international obligations and the domestic demands of an expanding economy.
(b)	To recommend with the least possible delay upon the basis of such investigation and examination how best this nation can meet the demands and obligations above-mentioned.
My proposal at that time was not made with a view to supplanting in any way the functions of provincial or dominion governments. What I had in mind was to find a way whereby, working together under our present

Conservation of Natural Resources system, we could obtain the maximum development of the objectives we had in mind. It was an attempt to co-ordinate the activities of governments at various levels in the hope that not only would we be able to meet in an orderly fashion the obligations placed upon us by our NATO commitments, but that we would be capable of handling our expanding economy at home, as well as looking sufficiently far into the future to meet conditions that might develop at that future time. Let us hope that the day may not be far distant when we may be in that position. We have to be ready for the day when the current international impasse will be at an end and we may return to a more normal state, although it may well be that the present industrial buoyancy resulting from defence preparedness may not be present then in the same degree as it is now. Let us hope that at such time we will be in a strong position to relate our economy to the needs of our own people, always keeping in mind our relations with other countries of the world as they may develop in the future.
It seemed to me that there was merit in the proposals I offered at that time. I felt that as a first move the provinces should be consulted, and that after such consultation the board might be set up for the purpose of making recommendations to bring about the desired objectives. I believe my suggestion has within it the germ of a program under which this country would move forward through concerted action, rather than by haphazard and piecemeal methods, both in the international and domestic fields. My suggestions had in mind no interference whatsoever with federal, provincial, municipal or private rights, but rather have for their purpose what might be described as Canadian team-play.
I believe any move in that direction should be welcomed by the government. I repeat the suggestion to the minister with all the conviction I can summon, because I feel there is need for this type of improvement, not only for the betterment of our own economy in Canada at this time but with a view to stabilizing our position internationally in the days that lie ahead.

They have not been declared to be common carriers. The same thing applies to natural gas. The pipe-line companies are being given the right to tap the natural gas and distribute it all over the country. We should not be patting ourselves on the back because of this type of development. I think the leader of the opposition missed the boat completely when he failed to realize that the system of free enterprise which he talks so much about has not been free enterprising enough in the way of supplying capital. We have had to import capital from the United States in order to develop our resources.
I submit that if risk capital could not be found in Canada to at least meet these basic requirements the Canadian government should have protected the Canadian people by retaining at least a 51 per cent interest in the capital invested in these resources in the name of the Canadian people. That could have been done, and I think it should have been done. The premier of Newfoundland is doing that kind of thing right now so far as bringing capital into that province by retaining 51 per cent of the shares, stock or capital going into such developments. I think it is something that is very necessary.
As I said when I rose, so far as thinking about the development of this country is concerned, it stops after you reach Quebec. I am glad to see the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) is now in his seat. He has a department under his control which is presumed to be concerned with the development of our resources; but it seems that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is the minister who actually has that power at the present time. I should like to call to the attention of the house the fact that within the last couple of months I had occasion to approach the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I was appealed to by a certain gentleman who had 57 square miles of territory, I think it was, leased in the province of Nova Scotia. He had tested that area and had found an excellent grade of iron ore.
All his tests were made and he had made a connection with a British company that took his samples and told him, according to the correspondence between them which I have read, that if he could develop that area the company would take one million tons a year of that grade of ore. The person who had the property under lease was not able to complete a certain survey that was necessary. He needed a magnetic survey of the area in order to complete the proving-up of the whole region. The Nova Scotia provincial government did not have that kind

After considerable delay I received a letter from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to the effect that they would not undertake that kind of survey for commercial purposes.
For what other purposes does the department make surveys? I hope it is not merely to put them in the archives. However, that is as far as I could get with the department. In the case to which I have referred this man carried on his own exploration for two years, had all his analyses made and finally came to the point where, in order to put the property under development and having an assured market for the product, all he needed was the help of the department in making a magnetic survey; and he was not able to get it.
I should like to ask the members from the maritimes if they think in that particular instance that part of the country is getting the kind of deal with respect to the development of its resources that the rest of Canada is getting. The minister clearly indicated that they opened a tungsten mine, I believe it was, in western Canada, operated it during the war and then sold it to a company. I imagine there was considerable capital invested there. When the war started they repurchased the mine, redeveloped it and put more capital into it. I imagine that millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money went into that development; but when the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is asked to do an ordinary routine job involving the use of equipment they already have one gets the short answer from the minister that they do not do that kind of survey for commercial purposes.

When the minister's estimates are before the house I hope he will let us know for what purpose they send out survey parties to search for new mineral deposits. Is it merely to get reports and then bury them in the archives, or is not the end in view, so far as all research, exploration and mapping is concerned, development for commercial purposes later on? I should like to get an answer from the minister to that question because I am sure the results of a large percentage of the research and exploration carried on by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are made available to the larger companies to help them in expansion and so forth.
My main reason for rising at this time was to bring up this matter. We hear discussions in the house year in and year out with regard to the development of the country, but they stop at Quebec. There is no thought of going east of Quebec. I have just mentioned the fact that I tried to get a little help from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to develop an industry that is badly needed in the maritimes, and I was lightly brushed off with the answer I have already given the house. As far as I am concerned, I cannot see the necessity for the amendment now before the house which has to do with developing our resources primarily for the benefit of Canada. Every possible development in this country, oil, coal and what have you, is already under lease either to Canadian capital or United States capital, but largely United States capital.
Let us take coal. In the maritimes the rights are under lease to the Dominion Coal Company for the next 99 years. There are parts of that section of the country where there are very good deposits of coal, but there is no capital in Canada with which to develop them. I could mention one example in the Inverness section. If the hon. member who represents that part of the country were in his seat he would tell you that for the past fifteen or twenty years that area has been a relief camp. There is an excellent grade of coal available there, but it will cost considerable money to develop it. We discussed that proposition in the reconstruction committee in 1942. We got an idea of the amount of capital necessary to develop it. The only

people in Canada who can supply the capital necessary to develop that area are the federal government, and the federal government is not going to undertake the project despite the fact that we import every year about 60 per cent of Canada's coal requirements. The federal government will not undertake that kind of development, and you cannot find in this country the kind of money necessary to undertake that kind of project.
The amendment suggests that the resources of the country should be developed by a combination of government and private enterprise, but I very much doubt whether you could find any resources in this country at the present time that are not already under lease. I cannot think of anything in the field of our basic resources that is not already leased to private capital in either Canada or the United States.
I do not agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this is a want of confidence motion. I think the motion and the amendment merely ask for the development of a policy in Canada that would urge the Canadian government and Canadian capital to take a greater part in the development of Canadian resources, with a guarantee that those resources are going to be owned, managed and distributed in Canada first on the basis of our own requirements, and secondly the surplus to outside countries.
I cannot see where there is any want of confidence. I think this business of leasing our resources to the United States leaves much to be desired. I understand a lot of people think it is wonderful that we brought our dollar back to par. The main reason the dollar came back to par is because of United States investment in this country. At the' same time my information is that in bringing the dollar back a little above par we have lost about $80 million in foreign exchange. There was that difference in our foreign exchange position. If our dollar has stepped up we have paid for it, if the press statement is true that there was that difference in our foreign exchange position.
I cannot see any reason why I cannot vote for this motion; but as far as I am concerned I am not satisfied with leasing Canadian resources to United States capital without the Canadian government taking some steps to protect Canadian people with respect to the future use of those resources. I believe that where we cannot find risk capital for development in this country, then the government of Canada should do what the government of Newfoundland is now doing; that is, hold at least 51 per cent of the shares, stocks

This debate is one I enter with protest because of the things that have been said. I am normally in quite fair agreement with my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), although I cannot but disagree with his interpretation of the United States capital invested in Canada. As a matter of fact, one thing that surprises me more than anything else is how little United States capital controls Canadian industry, how very little United States capital has recently entered Canada.
Figures in the millions or even in the billions are impressive, but compared with the new plant and the tremendous increase in gross national product, the percentage of United States investment in Canada has actually decreased since after the first war to the present time. It has decreased very considerably since the start of the second war. In other words, Canadian capital is now playing a very much larger part in the development of this country than it ever did before. Unfortunately I have not the figures with me, but I think I am safe in saying the percentage of United States capital, taken as a percentage either of the gross national product or of the capital value productive plant of this country, has decreased by as much as 35 per cent in the last ten years. I shall certainly ask the dominion bureau of statistics to get me those figures, and I would suggest that if any association can get them for a particular industry they would be extremely interesting. The point is that Canadian capital has led the field in this country. Canadian capital has done a job of development and Canadian capital is now doing a greater percentage of that development than it has ever done before.
Coming now to what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said this afternoon when he complained about the cutting of white pine up the Ottawa and Gatineau valleys:	True, the white pine was
cut; but it made the foundation of the building trade and the foundation of most of the construction of our cities and pioneer factories. Today the banks of the Ottawa river,

Conservation of Natural Resources far from being waste land, is good farm land; and from looking at them I would say they are being prosperously farmed all up and down the river at least on the Ontario side. Apart from that there has been probably the greatest hydroelectric development and capital investment on any river in the world. Again I would like somebody to compare the value of the trees, the white pine that has been cut, even at today's values, with the value of the electricity produced on those two rivers, the Gatineau and the Ottawa, in one single year. Far from leaving the valleys laid waste I do not think there is any valley in the world that has been so intensively developed. As a matter of fact, when I wish to show someone visiting Canada an area the development of which I am proud, I take them up the Ottawa river. I show them the tremendous capital development that has taken place in building those hydroelectric plants.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it will be said that they were developed by the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. That is true; but the point I wish to make is that while we have depleted our white pine resources we have in their stead a large farming area and the greatest hydroelectric development, as I have suggested, on any river in the world, with the possible exception of the Columbia.
Let us not belittle Canadians. Let us not say we have not done things when we have done them. Let us above all try to evaluate this matter of our natural resources and what we have done with them in a factual way.
There are two sides of this question of the depletion of natural resources, and there are two main theories that are being developed. One is the theory that has been put forward by Eugene Holman, who is president of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, in which he advances the idea that our natural resources are inexhaustible. He mentions oil, and I assume his figures are accurate, and states that for every barrel of oil that has been extracted in the last year, two barrels of potential oil have been discovered and brought into production. Not being an oil geologist I do not know the technical terms, but those are his figures, and I presume that as president of the world's largest oil company he knows what he is talking about.
I should like to quote what he says about the oil development in his article in the Atlantic Monthly for June. Speaking about oil he says the record-
... is one that shows that for every barrel of crude oil or cubic foot of natural gas withdrawn from the IMr. Adamson.]

ground in 1951, two new barrels of oil or cubic feet of gas were found or developed. Perhaps the idea is getting around.
I believe his concluding paragraph is of sufficient interest to the house to quote it. It reads as follows:
The basic requirement for progress is freedom- freedom to inquire, to think, to communicate, to venture. Without these conditions, the human mind and spirit will be so shackled that the availability of natural resources will be limited and we may exhaust the known sources of some needed material and find nothing to replace it. To the free man all things are possible. Opportunity is the wand which can change the useless into the useful, waste into raw materials of great value, exhaustible resources into inexhaustible resources. It is the key that unlocks the greatest energy source of all-the infinite power of the human individual.
The things which he regards as the shackling things are extreme nationalism, government control, monopoly, currrency restrictions, abnormal tariffs, threat of expropriation, wars and revolution. These are all the by-products of socialism. This is the argument of a petroleum chemist, who tells us that there will be and can be a continuing expansion of our natural resources. He believes that if one resource is depleted a substitute will be found through the genius of chemistry.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that on the basis of the record there is a tremendous amount in what this gentleman says. The improvement in our ability to refine and extract many minerals which we are now using so freely makes a big difference. Aluminum is an example. Today it is selling at 15 cents a pound; at the turn of the century it was selling for many dollars a pound. The ability of the mining industry, the ability of the chemist and the geologist to discover and extract all metals has reduced the price and made aluminum universally available. Titanium is another metal which we have recently discovered how to use. We may find that titanium will be a substitute for steel for certain uses. The chemist, the engineer and the research scientist have made it possible for this resource, known to us for many years, to become one of the great metal developments of this century.
So much for the man who believes that we have an inexhaustible store of resources. Let us look at the other side of the coin. Let us look at it from the point of view of this continent, and let us examine the metals in which Canada and the United States are deficient. Mr. Speaker, when the house rose I was just about to discuss the situation with regard to iron and steel in Canada in the light of our position as a North American country; because, whether we like it or not, we cannot defy geography. It is one of those things that are inescapable; and to try to divorce ourselves from the North American concept is not only ridiculous but impossible.
We have an economy that, until such time as atomic energy and nuclear fission take the place of the present sources of energy, must be built on the known fuels, and on basic steel. The figures I gave before recess regarding our North American deficiency position show that of the essential ingredients of a steel industry, we have to look forward to providing no less than seven of the alloys that go to make modern steel the effective metal it is. A steel industry is based on the essential ingredients of coal, iron ore and scrap. The basic components, in addition to these, of which we are deficient on this continent are manganese, fluorspar and graphite. Just to give an example of the importance of one small item, for the graphite used in the lining of the crucibles in which steel is poured we are dependent upon Madagascar and Ceylon. I mention this simply to show a tremendous job of research that might be done. If we could obtain a substitute for graphite, which is a small but essential ingredient in the process of steel making, we would forge one small link, nevertheless an essential link, in the whole process.
The components in which the American steel industry is deficient, are the following: chrome, manganese, nickel, cobalt, tungsten, molybdenum and vanadium. All these are essential in a steel industry for it is upon them that the maintenance of a modern steel industry depends. The challenge to us is to develop the seven alloy metals on which the whole complex economy of this continent depends. Unless we are prepared to be merely a producer of raw materials for others, a position which even in the days of confederation Sir John A. Macdonald rejected, the job lying ahead is much greater than anything we have met up to now.
A strange national psychology has been that we were a one-crop or one-product nation, one of the greatest errors we could make- and my authority for this statement is Dudley Stamp, in his book "Land of Tomorrow"-is to allow our western agriculture to remain a one-crop economy. We must begin to think in terms of a mixed farming economy in the west, just as we must continue to think of

a mixed manufacturing economy in the east and in the west, and not think as we did in the old days when manufacturing was done in the east and agriculture was confined to the west. I believe the great industrial revolution now taking place in the prairie provinces will soon adjust that balance.
The amendment contains a protest against what I like to call little Canadianism. We have this challenge; we have this responsibility as citizens of the world, not merely to produce the basic commodities but to find more of those basic commodities, to see that our resources are not depleted in respect of what we have and, furthermore, to see that everything we produce is used by us, not selfishly for our own good-because the world is too small for that-but so that everything we produce may reach its ultimate stage in Canada, so far as possible.
I have referred to 1975 as being the year when we will see a serious deficit position in the United States. This challenge is one which means that we must raise our sights with regard to population. It is one which means that we must raise our sights with regard to manufacturing and industry. It is one which demands that we must raise our sights with regard to the production of all raw materials. We cannot afford to waste anything. We cannot afford to leave any part of this country undeveloped or unexplored. If we do, we are not fulfilling our destiny; we are retrogressing and will become merely a producer of raw materials for others to use. That is a position I never want to see, a position which we in this house at this moment have a tremendous responsibility to prevent.

Mr. Speaker, the subject raised by the amendment is of vital importance to all Canadians; I feel that I should make an observation or two before a vote is taken on that amendment. In the main, members of the Social Credit group are in harmony with those who have spoken up to the present time. I should like to refer particularly to the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), with practically all of which I heartily agree. However, I felt the hon. member left the house and the country in some uncertainty about the oil situation in Alberta.
It seems to matter very little how often one puts the truth before the people, as some people seem to have a hard time getting it or believing those who tell it. The hon. member gave the idea that notwithstanding what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) had said, notwithstanding what I had said the other night, the Alberta government had alienated from the crown the lands on which

oil has been or is being found. That idea is absolutely fallacious. I hope that somehow or other we can impress upon our C.C.F. friends that the kind of thing they have been telling in Saskatchewan and British Columbia about what Alberta is doing with respect to oil is wrong.
Men who pretend to be as much interested in the development of Canadian resources and welfare as these gentlemen certainly can afford to tell the truth about what is being done in one province that is leading the way in respect to policies which they claim to be so interested in putting into operation in the country. One hon. member says that he has never mentioned oil. I am thankful that he is not responsible for the kind of thing I found in Saskatchewan a week ago. There certainly was some nonsense there, and the people who were spreading it seemed to be so sure they were right that you could not pound the truth into their heads with a claw hammer.

Conservation of Natural Resources in 1952, an absolutely authentic document. Dealing with natural resources, it states this on page 47:
No oil, mineral or timber bearing lands are sold. They are leased only for development on terms which ensure to all the people of the province a fair share of the development. The Alberta government's policy of giving encouragement to individual enterprise-co-operative as well as private- has proved beneficial in the interests of the people. The government does not risk the taxpayer's money in speculative enterprises. Monopoly control is prevented.
Once more that is a declaration that certainly anyone in this house and anyone attempting to be in public life ought to have the intelligence to understand and the honour to report correctly. On page 51 there is another comment which reads as follows:
Prior to 1941-maximum royalty from oil production on crown lands was 10 per cent. After 1941- royalty increased and placed on graduated scale with a maximum of 15 per cent and a minimum of 5 per cent dependent on average daily production with the option to the operator of paying 12J per cent of gross production until 1951. After June 1. 1951, royalty was placed on a sliding scale with a maximum of 163 per cent and minimum of 5 per cent dependent on the production of the well each month. Average royalty rate for latter half of 1951 was 14-1 per cent.
Here again is the clearest possible proof that the province has not in any way surrendered its rights to absolute control of its resources.
On page 55 of the document we find something pertaining to the protection of forests. With all that has been said in the house in this debate respecting the protection of Canadian forests I heartily agree. I believe we have been exceedingly remiss in our duty in this generation and in the generations immediately preceding ours, in the matter of conserving our forests. There are provinces where the reckless way in which lumbering and logging is permitted to go on I think constitutes a reflection on the intelligence of the people of those provinces, and an absolute disregard for the welfare of those who are to come in the future.
There are provinces in this dominion where 25 years from now I doubt very much that anyone will be able to get a piece of virgin timber to develop at all. I do not know how provision is being made for those who will come after us 50 years from now to obtain wood with which to build their homes. I am sure all this must stop. A public consciousness is developing, very slowly, in some parts of the country, which dictates to the people that they have a responsibility to their children and their children's children in the matter of conserving resources.

I will now read from page 55 of this document what Alberta does with respect to the protection of forests. It reads as follows:
The Alberta government has outlined a comprehensive program for the protection of forests and has taken definite action in this regard. Extensive areas have been set aside as permanent forested areas, in which no settlement will be permitted, and in which those engaged in lumbering operations will be required to follow a program of selective cutting and conservation. Restriction of settlement in the forested areas will not prevent development.
Negotiations carried out with the federal government resulted in a conservation program for the entire eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. Protection of this vast area is carried out by a special board.
May I interrupt for a moment to commend the responsible ministers of the government at Ottawa for the way in which they co-operated with Alberta in establishing protective measures on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. It was a fine, laudable thing which should produce rich results for those who come in the future. I continue:
The foremost objective is to stabilize and amplify the water supply for all the rivers watering the prairie plains. Experimental and research work is co-ordinated with the methods of the practical operator to learn the best logging practices. This will provide a supply of timber annually for the province's growing lumber industry, and with reforestation practices will ensure a perpetual source of supply.
I interrupt my reading to say that this constitutes an ideal state of affairs. It is a state of affairs which should prevail in every area across Canada from coast to coast. I go on:
An inventory of Alberta's forests started in 1949 and already 70,000 square miles have been photographed. Base maps and forest inventory maps are being prepared from these photographs. A forest surveys branch with a forest engineer in charge has been set up to handle the inventory and aerial photography in forest areas. Miles of roads, trails and telephone lines have been built in areas formerly inaccessible for fire fighting. Additional look-out towers and the installation of two-way radio facilities have furthered the safeguarding of this valuable natural resource, the forests of Alberta.
In the building of roads, exploring for oil, prospecting for ore, or for the extraction of lumber, aerial photographs are invaluable to the oil man, the lumberman, the surveyor or the engineer. Since the inception of the aerial photographic survey of the province by the department of lands and forests, 120,000 photographs now are available. Alberta is the first province to photograph aerially an entire province. The saving in time, money and energy of such a project will be a major factor in promoting and expanding the resources of this province.
May I interrupt to point out that this is one of the devices which have had such beneficial effects in the development of the Alberta oil industry. I believe that is sufficient to indicate the care that Alberta is taking. The document goes on to point out that very careful measures have been taken for the

preservation of game and fur-bearing animals and the increase thereof and that very adequate measures have been adopted, although in the beginning stages, in the development of Alberta fisheries and the protection thereof.
I am glad this debate has arisen. I wish that more positive and practical suggestions had been made by some of the speakers as to how the objectives they have in mind could be attained but, as I say, the debate was well worth while. We Social Crediters are heartily behind all wise measures for.the development of the nation's resources and the conservation thereof.

I would not wish to leave that on the record unchallenged. I did not attempt to go into the details of the tremendous iron possibilities across Canada. However, on many occasions I have made it clear that I am firmly convinced there are immense possibilities for the increased employment of our iron resources in every part of Canada. I hoped I had made it clear that I was not limiting my statement when I used the expression that a new iron ore empire has emerged right across Canada. I went further and spoke of the possibility of the greater use of our resources from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I mention that only for this reason, that I was not limiting my remarks in any way but stating a proposition which I believe applies to our iron ore resources right across the country.
I also wish to deal with one or two points made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I did not interrupt at the time he was speaking, but an interpretation was placed upon remarks I had made which I am sure those remarks did not support. He indicated that I had put forward a proposition that not a pound of iron ore should go to the United Kingdom. I said nothing of the kind. I said that the last pound of raw materials needed for the production of defence requirements should be assured. I did say that we should not encourage the export of a pound of iron ore that was not necessary for the defence purposes or that was not needed for the maintenance of continued production of essential requirements in another country. In fact I sought to make it clear that my position was the very contrary, and I believe these are the exact words I used. I said:
I hope that nothing I have said will be interpreted as an argument in favour of any dog-in-the-manger policy.
Conservation of Natural Resources
I had hoped my remarks from beginning to end indicated quite clearly that we should be prepared to accord those courtesies to the United Kingdom which we have received from them and also that we should co-operate with the United States in the great joint efforts we have made. I was directing my remarks particularly to the fact that we are expanding production of our raw materials at a tremendous rate, and I believe that in the increased production of these raw materials we should be directing our attention to the possibility of increasing the processing at advanced stages of all these raw materials for the greater employment of people in this country.
Referring to the subamendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell),
I would simply like to make a brief observation to explain why I do not propose to support it. If it were simply a deletion of those words with no explanation and nothing to indicate what the purpose of the deletion is, I might not object to voting for the motion in the amended form. The hon. member has very properly explained what he does mean by the subamendment. He has indicated that in moving this deletion it is an expression of his own objection to the advantage of the free enterprise system in the development of these resources.
When he criticizes what has happened under the free enterprise system in the development of these resources, and indicates perhaps not too explicitly that he thinks they could be better developed and processed under another system, I would point out that the abuses he is referring to have been abuses from the failure of governments to adequately supervise the use of those resources. I have indicated, without directing my criticism to any particular government, that in the very nature of things in a country with such abundant resources there has been a tendency to take them for granted; and undoubtedly at the government level and other levels there have been methods employed which should not be approved.
On the other hand I do not think the record of governments in supervising the use of these resources in itself is a very good argument in favour of giving still greater authority to a government not only to supervise but to go apparently a step further and to engage in processing as well. It was for that very reason that this motion sought to make it clear in advocating the further processing, as well as the conservation of these resources, we believe it is under the free

Conservation of Natural Resources enterprise system that this work will best be carried on and the highest measure of employment will be created.
That does not in any way overlook the abuses that have threatened some of our resources in the past. Nor does it in any way lessen the weight of my own contention that we should use our resources with the utmost care. I do believe, however, that it is the function of government to supervise, and that the actual processing and manufacturing can be carried out by private enterprise to the greatest advantage of our people. For that reason I do not intend to support the subamendment.
The motion by way of amendment is clearly intended to assert the proposition that under adequate plans for conservation and supervision we believe we should rely on the enterprise and energy of free men and women in building up the various activities of this country.
There is one other point I wish to touch, and it was raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). He raised the question whether this motion which I have moved by way of an amendment in any way interfered with the plans for leasing the property now leased in different parts of this country, as distinguished from outright grants. I want to leave no doubt that I am not putting forward any proposition that any plans or any policy for the development of our resources should at any time be permitted to infringe upon the jurisdiction of the provincial governments over the resources that have been placed under their control.
Some of those resources are leased in different parts of the country. Others have been granted for development. I think it is quite clear that the dominion government and the parliament of Canada must not interfere with the rights of the provincial governments and the provincial legislatures to determine how they will deal with their own resources. For that reason I would point out to the hon. member for Peace River that I naturally am not only supporting but emphasizing that the plans worked out in any province for the handling of their resources must be respected and preserved.
I can only once more point out what I said in my earlier remarks, that I had hoped the proposal put forward would be regarded as a constructive proposal, and that it need not be looked upon as criticism of what has happened in the past under this or any other government. We have entered a period where there is going to be a tremendous demand on our resources because of the unusual world demand. That demand is going to be enormously increased, as was

pointed out by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), who placed before this house figures showing that in the comparatively near future there is going to be such a serious deficiency of raw materials in the United States that pressures are going to mount to a still greater level for the supply of raw materials from Canada.
We wish to co-operate with our friends and neighbours in every way, but I repeat what I said at the outset. In presenting this motion I believe the first concern of the government of Canada and the parliament of Canada should be the welfare of the people of Canada. I believe, therefore, that there should be a clearly stated policy that while we are prepared to export our resources under arrangements that will meet proper demands in keeping with the resources we possess, at the same time we should make sure that in every way possible those resources will be processed and manufactured to a very high level so that wages can be paid to Canadian workmen and so that employment may be expanded and increased throughout the whole of this country.

Northwest Territories Act would think it would be within that framework that you would resolve the problem you gave to us the other day as to the extent of debate which should be allowed.

Northwest Territories Act of view it is not a debate at all. Mr. Chairman, the continued growth of Canada's north was the underlying reason why the government, during the first session last year, asked parliament to pass a number of amendments to the Northwest
Northwest Territories Act Territories Act to bring it more into line with present-day conditions. The principal amendment at that time was one empowering the citizens of the Northwest Territories to elect three members to the Northwest Territories council, whose total membership is eight. Since that time a careful study has been made of the apportionment of responsibilities between the federal government and the territorial government. It is now proposed to transfer additional revenues to the territorial government and to place upon it additional responsibilities more in keeping with its new status.
It is proposed to confer upon the commissioner in council of the territories legislative jurisdiction in several matters which are now not assigned to it; to provide for the establishment of a territorial revenue account; to re-establish the territorial court to facilitate the administration of justice.
In one of the amendments last year provision was made to pay to each elected member of the council the actual travelling expenses incurred by him in travelling from his place of residence to the place where the council holds its session, and return; and also an allowance for living expenses not exceeding $15 for each day during which the council is in session. For a variety of reasons the amount established to cover living expenses is not considered to be adequate, and it is proposed to increase it. It is proposed also to make a number of other minor changes to the act.
The proposed legislation will be in the form of a consolidation of the present act of 1927 and the four amending acts passed in 1938, 1940, 1948, and 1951.

On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to delay the progress of the committee with respect to this measure. I rise only to indicate that not only was this bill which is to implement the treaty of peace between Canada and Japan studied by the standing committee on external affairs, but that committee also had before it the treaty itself, which was fully discussed.
The deliberations in the committee were centred around inquiries of various governmental representatives from the Department of External Affairs, the department of immigration, the Department of Trade and Commerce and others. Perhaps the main interest of the committee was in the questions of trade and immigration, as one might expect having in mind the character of the relationship between Canada and Japan in previous times.
The main contention which arose in the committee had to do with section 4 and this resulted in a vote on the question of whether

or not the governor in council had been given too much power and parliament too little, if I may put it in those oversimplified terms. During the progress of this discussion I think the hon. member for Eglinton may have a word with respect to clause 4, because he was the member who took the initiative concerning this matter. With the exception of that feature I think the committee presented a somewhat unanimous front with respect to the treaty itself. While there were certain items in it which of course caused the committee some concern, as no doubt they cause the government a good deal of concern, nevertheless on balance the treaty was endorsed. In addition so was Bill No. 210, the issue having been decided against those who thought there should have been a change in clause 4. I do not think there is any point in my elaborating on the committee's work or in making any further observations.

maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT
speechtext: For quite a long time now there have been indications that once this treaty with Japan had been ratified an attempt would be made to bring about substantial immigration of Japanese to Canada. The lead in this direction has been taken by the national Japanese-Canadian citizens' association.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT

maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT

maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT

maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TREATY OF PEACE (JAPAN) ACT PROVISIONS FOR CARRYING TREATY INTO EFFECT
